title: Orange Pi 3B: From Your Computer to Your First Web Page
description: Understand the five parts that actually do the work, and follow how a system image travels from a Windows computer to a web page you can open in a browser.
keyInsight: The development board does not do this alone: the computer prepares the boot medium, the board loads Linux, the local network opens a remote channel, and Nginx finally sends the page back to the browser.

nodes.label: Your First Orange Pi Web Page
nodes.summary: Write the system to a TF card, start the board, install Nginx through SSH, and view the page in a browser.
nodes.function: Connect preparation, startup, networking, remote control, and web-page acceptance into one working path.
nodes.source: orange-pi-3b-codex-guide.md

nodes.label: Computer
nodes.summary: Prepare the image, identify the TF card, write it, and finally open SSH and the web page.
nodes.function: Acts as the control desk for the whole process: stores files, runs the writing tool, accepts commands, and shows results.
nodes.source: Guide: local file inventory, disk identification, and Windows clients

nodes.label: TF Card System

nodes.function: Turns a downloaded image into partitions, boot files, and a Linux root file system that the board can read directly.
nodes.source: Guide: image selection, SHA256 check, writing, and verification

nodes.label: Orange Pi Host and Power

edges.explanation: The computer first verifies the image and TF card, then uses the image writer to copy the image block by block, turning an ordinary storage card into a boot system the Orange Pi can read.
Insert the written and verified TF card into the unpowered board. After power-on, the Orange Pi reads its boot files, Linux kernel, and root file system from the card.
After Linux starts and activates the network interface, the host requests a local address from the router. Once the user finds that IP, Windows can locate and log in to the board through SSH.
SSH sends installation and configuration commands to the board. After Nginx starts listening for HTTP requests, the Windows browser uses the same local IP to fetch and display the custom page.
The verified local image file becomes the input to the image writer.
The image writer should write to the TF card only after the user has manually confirmed the disk's identity.
Writing creates a bootable system; only then do the terminal and browser have a remote target to connect to.
The image is copied block by block to the TF card, recreating its predefined partitions and files.
The card reader lets Windows recognize and write to the TF card.
After writing, the TF card contains the board's boot partition and Linux file system.
The board's chip reads the TF card in boot order and gradually hands control to the system.
Stable power continuously supplies the energy needed to read storage, initialize hardware, and load the kernel.
When the boot chain finishes, Linux is ready for login, networking, and running services.
The board sends a DHCP request through the Ethernet cable, and the router returns an IP usable on the local network.
The user puts the confirmed board IP into the SSH command so the connection has a definite target.
The SSH service on the board verifies the user and creates a remote command-line session.
After the package is installed, systemd can start and manage the Nginx process.
Running Nginx reads the site file and converts it into an HTTP response.
When the browser displays the custom content, it proves that the response path and the entire preceding chain work end to end.
Physical-disk information and volume/drive-letter information complement each other.
After reviewing the physical-disk and volume information together, the user makes the final confirmation of the target TF card.
Only a download that explicitly supports Orange Pi 3B is accepted as a candidate.
The local image must pass the SHA256 comparison before it can move to the writing step.
The boot content read from the TF card locates and loads the Linux kernel.
After the kernel initializes hardware and mounts the file system, it starts user-space services.
The first SSH connection returns the remote host fingerprint for the user to confirm.
After accepting the correct host fingerprint and completing authentication, the user enters the remote shell.
The HTML file content is placed in the body of the HTTP response returned by Nginx.
After receiving the response, the browser parses the HTML and forms the page the user can see.
